We have already explained that, wherever the appearance of an angel or an address made by him is spoken of, it can only be a matter of a *prophetic vision* or a *dream*[^1], regardless of whether it has been expressly declared or not, as has been previously stated. It is necessary to know this and to be well imbued with it. It matters little whether it is said at first of someone that he saw the angel, or whether it seems to be said that he took him at first for a human individual, and that in the end it became manifest to him that it was an angel[^2]; as soon as you find in the denouement that he who was seen and who spoke was an angel, you shall know and be certain that from the beginning it was a *prophetic vision* or a *prophetic dream*. Indeed, in the prophetic vision or in the prophetic dream, at times the prophet sees God who speaks to him, as we shall explain; at other times he sees an angel who speaks to him; at other times he hears someone who speaks to him, without seeing the person who speaks; and finally, at other times he sees a human individual who addresses him, and afterwards it becomes manifest to him that he who spoke was an angel[^3]. In prophecy of this last species, he relates that he saw a man act or speak, and that afterwards he knew that it was an angel.

[^1]: That is to say, of a state where the imaginative faculty prevails over the perception of the senses.
[^2]: As, for example, the *three men* whom Abraham saw (Genesis 18:2), and the *man* whom Joshua saw (Joshua 5:13).
[^3]: On these different degrees of prophecy, see below, chap. XLV.

It is this important principle[^1] that was professed by one of the doctors, and even one of the greatest among them, namely R. ’Hayya the Great, concerning this passage of the Pentateuch: *And the Lord appeared unto him in the Oaks of Mamre, etc.* (Genesis 18:1); for, after having first said summarily that God appeared to him, one begins by explaining under what form this appearance took place, and it is said that he saw at first three men, that he ran (to meet them), that they spoke and that they were spoken to[^2]. He, therefore, who gives this interpretation says that these words of Abraham: *Lord! if I have found favor in thy sight, do not pass thus before thy servant* (ibid., v. 3) are also an account of what, in the prophetic vision, he said to one of them: "It was," he says, "to the greatest among them that he addressed the word[^3]." It is also necessary to be well imbued with this subject, for it contains a profound mystery[^4].

[^1]: That is to say, this principle that, in all the appearances related in one of the four ways just spoken of, it is a matter of a vision or a dream.
[^2]: The editions of the version of Ibn-Tibbon bear ואמרו מאמר אליהם; the word מאמר is but a printing error for ונאמר. Al-’Harizi translates: ודברו עמו והשיב להם.
[^3]: See *Beréschîth rabbâ*, sect. 48 (fol. 42, col. 4). — This passage is very obscure; for one does not understand how the author found all that he says here in the few words of R. ’Hayya, which appear to have no other purpose than to explain the use of the singular in verse 3, while in the following verses Abraham addresses the three angels at once and always speaks in the plural. R. ’Hayya says, therefore, that Abraham addressed the word to the principal among them, who was Michael. To resolve the difficulty, Abravanel (Commentary on the *Moreh*, II, fol. 40 a) thinks that one must refer to the two opinions emitted by the doctors on the word אדני, *Lord*, employed in verse 3; according to some, this word replaces the *tetragrammaton* name of verse 1 and designates God Himself; according to others, it designates one of the *three men* of whom verse 2 speaks. According to the first opinion, the vision, in which Abraham represented in his mind God Himself, or the *supreme cause*, would have been interrupted by the appearance of the *three men*, and Abraham, distracted by this appearance, would have prayed God not to depart from him, that is to say, that he would have made efforts not to allow himself to be interrupted in his contemplation of the Divinity. According to the second opinion, the appearance of the three men would be identical with that of God, of which verse 1 speaks; so that verse 2 and the following would only explain in detail the nature of the divine manifestation of verse 1. Now, R. ’Hayya, evidently professing the second opinion, it follows that, according to him, all the details related from verse 2 onwards are a prophetic vision, in the same right as the appearance of God in verse 1, which would only summarize the whole of the details that follow. — Doubtless, this is to explain with too much subtlety the simple words of R. ’Hayya; but it is conformable to the manner in which Maimonides, in general, interprets the often so naive words of the ancient doctors.
[^4]: Literally: *for it is a mystery among mysteries*. The version of Ibn-Tibbon bears: בםוד מן הםודות; instead of בםוד (mss. כםור), one must read בי הוא םוד, as in the version of Al-’Harizi. — The mystery of which the author wishes to speak is that all the details related in chap. XVIII of Genesis, the meal which the *three men* ate, the words they addressed to Sarah, etc., did not actually happen and took place only in the imagination of Abraham, i.e., in a prophetic vision. It is the same, as the author is about to say, with the wrestling of the angel with Jacob, with what happened to Bileam with his she-ass, with the angel who appeared to Joshua before Jericho, and with many other biblical narratives, which must be considered as prophetic visions. This opinion, as one may well think, has found, among Jewish theologians, numerous contradictors. See notably the polemic of R. Moses ben-Nahman, in his commentary on Genesis, at chap. XVIII.

I say likewise that, in the history of Jacob, when it is said: *And a man wrestled with him* (ibid., XXXII, 25), it is a matter of a prophetic revelation, since it is clearly said at the end (verses 29 and seq.) that it was an angel. It is exactly as in the history of Abraham, where it is first related summarily that *God appeared to him etc.*, and afterwards one begins to explain how that occurred. Likewise, concerning Jacob, it is said (at first): *Angels of God met him* (ibid., v. 2); then one begins to set forth what occurred until the moment when *they met him*, and it is said that he sent messengers (to Esau), and that after having acted and having done (such and such a thing), *Jacob remained alone etc.* (ibid., v. 25); for here it is a matter of those same angels of God of whom it was first said *angels of God met him*[^1], and this wrestling, as well as the entire dialogue (which follows), took place in a *prophetic vision*. Likewise, all that occurred with Bileam *on the way* (Numbers 22:22 and seq.), as well as the discourse of the she-ass, (all that, I say,) took place in a prophetic vision[^2], since it is expressly said at the end (verse 32) that the *angel of the Lord* spoke to him[^3]. Likewise again, concerning these words (from the book) of Joshua (5:13), *he lifted up his eyes and saw that a* MAN *stood over against him*, I say that this took place in the prophetic vision, since it is clearly said afterwards (v. 14 and 15) that it was *a captain of the host of the Lord*. — [As for this passage *And a* MALAKH (messenger) *of the Lord came up from Gilgal etc. And it came to pass, when the* MALAKH *of the Lord spake these words unto all Israel* (Judges 2:1 and 4), the doctors have written that *the* MALAKH *of the Lord* spoken of here is Phinehas; they express themselves thus: "it is Phinehas, who, at the moment when the divine majesty rested upon him, resembled a *malakh* (angel) of the Lord[^4]."]

[^1]: The author means that in verse 25, where it is said: *Jacob being left alone, a man wrestled with him*, one must see, in the *man who wrestled*, one of the *angels of God* spoken of in verse 2.
[^2]: It must be recalled here that, according to the ancient Jewish doctors, the gift of prophecy was granted also to certain pagan sages, who had for their mission to predict the fortune of the people of Israel. See what is said, concerning Bileam, in the *Midrash* of Leviticus or *Wayyikra rabbâ*, sect. 1 (fol. 147, col. 1), and in the *Midrash* of the Song of Songs, or *Schîr ha-schîrîm rabbâ*, at chap. II, v. 3 (fol. 9, col. 4).
[^3]: Which, as the author says at the beginning of this chapter, indicates a dream, or a prophetic vision.
[^4]: This citation is not textual; for the author appears to have in view the following passage from *Wayyikra rabbâ*, sect. 1 (fol. 146, col. 1): וכי מלאך היה והלא פינחס היה ולמה קורא אותו מלאך אלא אמר ר׳ סימון פינחס בשעה שהיתה רוח הקדש שורה עליו פניו בוערות כלפידים.

We have already explained that the name of *malakh* is homonymous, and that the prophet also is called *malakh*[^1], as, for example, in the following passages: *He sent a* MALAKH *and brought us forth out of Egypt* (Numbers 20:16); *Then spake Haggai, the* MALAKH *of the Lord, in the Lord's message* (Haggai 1:13); *And they mocked the* MALAKHIM (*messengers*) *of God* (II Chronicles 36:16).] — When Daniel says: *And Gabriel, that personage whom I had seen at first in a vision, arrived at me in a swift flight, toward the time of the evening oblation* (Daniel 9:21),
